title: Grammar Terms: Clauses and Conjunctions
keyIdea: A clause is a group of words with a verb: the dog barked. A phrase has no verb: after lunch. A main clause makes sense on its own. A subordinate clause, such as because it rained, leaves you waiting and needs a main clause. Conjunctions join clauses. Coordinating conjunctions (and, but, or, so) join two equal clauses. Subordinating conjunctions (because, when, if, although) start a subordinate clause, which can often move to the front with a comma.

kid: A clause is a group of words with a verb in it. The verb is the doing or being word. The dog barked is a clause, because barked is the verb. After lunch has no verb, so it is a phrase.

Some clauses make sense on their own. We stayed in. That is a main clause. Other clauses leave you waiting. Because it rained... what happened? That is a subordinate clause. It needs a main clause to lean on.

Conjunctions join clauses. And, but, or and so join two main clauses that are equal. Because, when, if and although start a subordinate clause. Try the flip test: Because it rained, we stayed in. It still works, so because is subordinating.
Watch out for words like after and until. In after we ate, a verb comes next, so after is a conjunction. In after lunch, there is no verb, so after is a preposition.
adult: The English National Curriculum lists clause, subordinate clause, conjunction and preposition as Year 3 grammar terms in English Appendix 2, building on Year 2 work on co-ordination (or, and, but) and subordination (when, if, that, because). The US Common Core standard L.3.1h asks pupils to use coordinating and subordinating conjunctions, L.3.1i to produce simple, compound and complex sentences, and L.4.1f to correct fragments.

Teach the tests rather than lists. Has it got a verb? Then it is a clause. Can it stand alone? Then it is a main clause. Can the conjunction and its clause move to the front? Then the conjunction is subordinating, and a comma follows the fronted clause. Coordinating conjunctions such as but and so fail that flip test.

Common mistakes: writing a subordinate clause alone as a sentence ('Because the bus was late.'), thinking the clause that comes first must be the main one, and calling every joining word an 'and word'. Pupils also confuse prepositions with conjunctions, since after, before and until can be both. The word that follows decides: a clause makes it a conjunction, a phrase makes it a preposition.

In the lab your child taps the verb to tell clauses from phrases, picks the main clause in three sentences, mends three fragments by adding a main clause, uses the flip test to sort four conjunctions as coordinating or subordinating, and decides whether after and until are conjunctions or prepositions.

familyTip: Say a subordinate clause like "When I got home" and stop. Your child adds a main clause to finish it: "When I got home, I ate a snack." Then swap roles and try the flip test together.

visual.caption: Coordinating or subordinating? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: tell clauses from phrases, find main clauses, fix fragments, flip-test conjunctions and spot when after is a preposition.

practice.prompt: In "We stayed in because it rained", which part is the main clause?
practice.hint: Which part makes sense as a sentence on its own?
practice.explain: "We stayed in." makes sense alone, so it is the main clause. "Because it rained" is a subordinate clause that leaves you waiting.

practice.prompt: Each clause has one verb. A sentence has {n} verbs, each in its own clause. How many clauses does it have?
practice.explain: With one verb in each clause, {n} verbs means {n} clauses.

practice.prompt: Which word is a subordinating conjunction?
practice.hint: Try the flip test. Which word can move to the front with its clause?
practice.explain: "Although it was cold, we played out" still works, so although is subordinating. But and or are coordinating.

practice.prompt: A long sentence has {n} clauses. Only one of them is the main clause. How many subordinate clauses does it have?
practice.hint: Take the one main clause away from the total.
practice.explain: {n} clauses take away 1 main clause leaves {=n-1} subordinate clauses.

pool.hint: Look for a doing word, a verb. A clause has one; a phrase does not.
pool.explain: Laughed is a verb, so "the baby laughed" is a clause. The other two have no verb, so they are phrases.

choices: When the film ended, we went home.
pool.hint: A full sentence needs a main clause.
pool.explain: Only the first has a main clause, "we went home". The others are fragments.

pool.prompt: In "If it is sunny, we will go to the park", which part is the subordinate clause?
choices: we will go to the park
pool.explain: "If it is sunny" cannot stand alone, so it is the subordinate clause, even though it comes first.

pool.prompt: In "She smiled after she won", what job does "after" do?
pool.hint: Is there a verb in the words after it?
pool.explain: "she won" has the verb won, so it is a clause. After joins it on, so it is a conjunction.

pool.prompt: In "She smiled after the race", what job does "after" do?
pool.hint: Is there a verb in the words after it?
pool.explain: "the race" has no verb, so it is a phrase. Here after is a preposition.

pool.prompt: Which word joins two equal main clauses?
pool.explain: But is a coordinating conjunction. Because and if start subordinate clauses.

pool.prompt: You join {n} main clauses into one sentence, putting "and" between each pair. How many times do you write "and"?
pool.hint: Draw the clauses in a row and count the gaps between them.
pool.explain: {n} clauses in a row have {=n-1} gaps, so you write and {=n-1} times.

pool.prompt: A story has {a} subordinate clauses. Each one needs its own main clause to make a sentence. How many main clauses do you need at least?
pool.hint: Pair each subordinate clause with one main clause.
pool.explain: One main clause for each subordinate clause means at least {a} main clauses.
